text.p: Metal prices staged an impressive comeback on the London Metal Exchange on Wednesday, whipping back to post fresh highs in copper and aluminium.
Gold and wheat closed weaker but oil prices firmed.
The CRB Index rose 1.28 points to 242.9.
METALS

The LME metals complex scored an impressive comeback by Wednesday's close. After prices slumped on Tuesday, traders and analysts expected the market to test the downside or at least consolidate for several days. But after a quick probe lower in the morning, prices snapped back, led by nickel, forcing shorts to scramble to cover and sparking a widespread rally.
Nickel led the turnaround in the morning when unhappy workers at the huge Norilsk complex in Russia threatened to strike on March 15 over unpaid wages.

The slide in three month prices screeched to a halt at a low of $7,760 and emboldened the other metals to also reverse direction as funds and speculative players were forced to cover their short positions.
"Consumer buying, while not the main element, also added to the euphoria," said analyst Robin Bahr at broker Brandeis.
Nickel regained the $8,000 break-out point and finished just off its high at $8,050, a gain of $200 on the day.
If the market is able to hold above $8,000, it should be on track to rechallenge recent highs of $8,120, analysts said.
Above there were targets of $8,200, highs from May 1996 and $8,430, the May 14 peak.
Three months copper ended the kerb $42 higher at $2,392 per tonne, just $1 off its a fresh nine-month high, after sliding to a low of $2,335 in the morning.
Later, in inter-office trading the market shot up further to be bid above $2,400.
The next major chart level was seen at $2,434, the high of June 4, 1996, and a $2,450 technical target from an ascending triangle.
Wider spreads and borrowing of March/April gave an added boost to the market. The premium of cash over three months widened to $67/$70 from $60/65 on Tuesday.
Aluminium also scored fresh highs, hitting a 9-1/2 month peak of $1,665 and ending the kerb there, up $22 on the day.
Chartists peg the next significant level at $1,680, the high of May 1996.
Zinc also joined in the fun, regaining the $1,200 area and ending the kerb $14 higher at $1,222.
This put it on line to rechallenge the recent high of $1,235 and the January 1995 peak of $1,239, analysts said.
The other metals were less buoyant. Lead ended $1 higher at $665 and tin showed independence by ignoring the gains in the others. It lost $69 to end the kerb at $5,841.
GOLD

NYMEX platinum group metals futures (PGMs) ended sharply higher Wednesday, helped by further news of a threatened strike at Russia's Norilsk mine from March 15, but COMEX gold and silver futures ended lower. NYMEX April platinum ended up $4.90 an ounce at $386.70, after seeing a 12-week high at $388.00 intraday. Comex April gold closed down 10 cents at $356.20 an ounce after first seeing a 20-day intraday high at $358.70, though resistance is still seen around $360.00, traders said. Spot gold bullion ended quoted $354.00/50, compared to the London Wednesday afternoon fix at $354.75 and the New York close Tuesday at $354.00/50. CHICAGO - Reminders of stiff export competition, a downward correction in the soy complex and confirmation Canada was railing wheat to be shipped through a U.S. port pressured CBOT wheat futures to a lower close, traders said. The Canadian Wheat Board said Wednesday it is shipping an "average sized" cargo load of wheat to Portland. Also a Philippine firm rejected bids for 40,000 tonnes of U.S. wheat, Manila traders said, and there was news Japan agreed to buy 900,000 tonnes of wheat from Australia in calendar 1997. Wheat closed 1-1/2 to 6-1/4 cents per bushel lower, with March down 6-1/4 at $3.70-3/4.
OIL

NYMEX crude ended higher Wednesday, bucking declines in the rest of the oil complex, after an Iraqi Kurdish group said rival Kurds and Iraqi forces were preparing for a possible attack against it. "It may have some sort of basis in fact, but whether it leads to anything unusual in Iraq and affects (oil) supply is another story," said Tim Evans, analyst with Pegasus Econometric Group in New York. "The market decided it's worth a little more than 10 cents, and that seems about right," said Evans. April crude settled up 11 cents at $21.11 a barrel.
SUGAR

CSCE world sugar futures settled near the day's highs, buoyed by late-session speculative buying and interest from Far Eastern dealers in the March/May spread. Floor traders viewed the settlement as bullish for prices, citing a close near the day's highs despite the week's low of 10.75 cents hit early in the session. May ended at a 0.01 cent premium to March compared with a 0.03 cent premium on Tuesday. The most-active contract closed 0.06 cent higher at 10.89, having ranged form 10.91 to 10.75 cents. March settled up 0.10 cent to 10.90.
